title: Al-Malik, the King
hook: the King, owner of everything, and so nothing is really yours

segments.voice: Yesterday, rahmah: mercy in a hundred parts, and mercy that outruns anger. Your line was mercy wins.

A library book can go everywhere with a person for three weeks. It gets read in bed and on the bus, a corner folded with a twinge of guilt. It starts to feel like theirs. Then the due date comes, and it goes back, because it never was. In Medina, a woman named Umm Sulaym lost her little son while her husband, Abu Talha, was away. When he came home, she fed him and let him rest. Then, Sahih Muslim reports, she asked him: if people lent something to a family, and then asked for it back, would the family have the right to refuse?
screen: `A LIBRARY BOOK, DUE BACK.` → `UMM SULAYM'S QUESTION.` → `CAN YOU REFUSE TO RETURN A LOAN?`

segments.voice: No, said Abu Talha. Then, she said, seek your reward with Allah for your son. He was upset that she had waited to tell him, and he went to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who prayed for blessing on the two of them. Her question holds today's name. Al-Malik comes from the root m-l-k: to own, to possess, to rule. The same root gives malik, king, and mulk, sovereignty. In the Fatiha, one line has two accepted readings: Maliki yawm id-din, King of the Day of Judgment, and Maaliki, Owner of it. Both are recited, the meanings held together. The Qur'an names Him al-Malik in al-Hashr; Pickthall has: He is Allah, than Whom there is no other God, the Sovereign Lord. And in an-Nas, the King of mankind. Bukhari and Muslim record the Prophet describing the Day when Allah will fold up the heavens, take the earth in His hand, and say: I am the King. Where are the kings of the earth? Every crown and title, gone quiet. If He is the Owner, what a person calls mine is held on loan: the house, the phone, the body, even the children they love. That doesn't make things cheap; a borrowed thing is treated with care. It loosens the grip. At any loss, Muslims say words from al-Baqarah that Pickthall renders: Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning. This week began with the beautiful names, the name of names, and mercy vast and near. It ends with the King.
screen: `SEEK YOUR REWARD FOR YOUR SON.` · `M-L-K — TO OWN, TO RULE.` · `WHERE ARE THE KINGS OF THE EARTH?` · `WHAT'S MINE IS HELD ON LOAN.` · then, large: `EVERYTHING IS LENT.`

segments.voice: Hold something small you think of as yours, your phone, your keys, a ring, a cup, in your open hand, and say quietly: this is lent to me, noticing what stirs in your chest, resistance or relief. Then set it down gently, rest your hands on your knees, and notice that your hands are lent too. If you pray, you can say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un.
Al-Malik. The King, the Owner of everything, so that all we hold is lent, to be cared for and one day returned. Today's word.
Your line: everything is lent. Hold it like a library book. That's a week of names.

howItsDone: Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un (we belong to Allah and to Him we return) at news of any loss, from a death to a broken cup, and wealth, family and life are often spoken of as an amanah, a trust held for a time.

chat.says: If God is al-Malik, the Owner, what does that mean for what I own?
options: It's lent to you: cared for, held loosely, and one day given back.
It's worthless, so there's no need to look after any of it.
It's a reward you earned, so it's yours to keep forever.
chat.meaning: If He is the Owner, what we call mine is on loan: not cheap, but treated with care and held loosely.
